newsitem.title: THAILAND: Latest crackdown shows Burma military insecure.
newsitem.headline: Latest crackdown shows Burma military insecure.

text.p: Burma's latest crackdown on the democracy movement and rare student protests show its military rulers are worried the two forces could merge and become a source of trouble, diplomats said on Thursday.
The crackdown also signalled that the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) was insecure despite its firm grip on power, they told Reuters.

They said the fact the government was trying to link the democracy movement with the student demonstrations -- which were held to protest the way police handled a non-political argument between students and restaurant owners -- was a sign of the government's insecurity.
There are no formal links between university students in Burma and the democracy movement because most students say they are afraid to get involved in politics.
"I think the government is paranoid the two will come together," said one Rangoon-based diplomat. "That's why they have arrested U Kyi Maung."

Kyi Maung, a close confidant of democracy leader Aung San Suu Kyi and a top official in her National League for Democracy (NLD) party, was picked up for questioning on Wednesday morning for his involvement in the student protests.

A senior government official told Reuters on Thursday that Kyi Maung was being detained because he had talked for an hour with two student leaders on Tuesday. He did not say when Kyi Maung would be released.
The government accused the NLD, and specifically Kyi Maung, of colluding with the students to try and create unrest.
Political analysts said the SLORC was probably unnerved by the similarity between the argument on Sunday that sparked the protest and a teashop quarrel in 1988.

In 1988, a scuffle between students and shop owners in a teashop sparked nationwide outrage against the previous military government, leading to pro-democracy street demonstrations that left thousands dead or in jail.

The scuffle on Sunday between three students from the Yangon Institute of Technology (YIT) and restuarant owners resulted first in a sit-in on Tuesday then a major sit-in demonstration by up to 1,000 people early on Wednesday.
The students say the demonstrations were apolitical.

They said they were staged to protest the violent way the three students were handcuffed and treated by police before being eventually freed, and the inaccurate way the scuffle was reported in national media.
The SLORC said in a statement the protests were a ruse to foment unrest among students and the Burmese people.
"I think there are people among them who are agitating, although most of the students just want to pursue their studies," the government official told Reuters.

He said the situation was different from that in 1988 because the SLORC, which seized power after the 1988 protests, was in firm control now while in 1988 there was widespread discontent with the previous government's policies.

But most diplomats said it was unclear why the students -- who have been closely monitored since their strong role in the 1988 uprisings -- would hold a large protest in the street and hope it would not be seen as a political statement.
"It's all a lot of really weird stuff going on," one Rangoon-based diplomat said. "We haven't worked out who is behind it and why it's happening right now."
